title: The history of the drone
tagline: From a radio-controlled boat in 1898 to the quadcopters that map Indian villages and carry vaccines.
intro: Remote control began on the water and in the air with radio signals, and the first pilotless aircraft were built in the First World War. Target drones came in the 1930s and 1940s. The quadcopter arrived when cheap sensors could keep four rotors level, and India has since written rules for the zones and the registration that every drone must follow.

eras.name: Radio control and first flights
eras.summary: Tesla's patent, the first pilotless flights and the target drones of the Second World War.

eras.name: Cheap sensors and cameras
eras.summary: Toy quadcopters gain cameras, and cheap gyroscopes make flight control small enough for every drone.

eras.name: India writes its rules
eras.summary: The Drone Rules, the airspace map, the certification scheme and the amendments that followed.

eras.name: Drones at work
eras.summary: Schemes for farmers, villages and remote areas use drones for spraying, mapping and small deliveries.

events.title: A vessel steered from a distance
events.text: Nikola Tesla received US Patent 613,809 for controlling a vessel's propulsion and steering from outside it. It is one of the earliest patents for radio-style remote control of a moving machine.
events.why: Every drone is a machine steered by signals from a pilot who is not on board.

events.title: The Kettering Bug takes to the air
events.who: Charles Kettering and the Dayton engineers
events.text: The Kettering Bug, a small pilotless biplane, made its first flight on 2 October 1918, and that flight failed: it climbed too steeply, stalled and crashed. About 45 were built by the end of the war, and none were used in combat.
events.why: It showed that an aircraft could fly without a pilot on board, with its control set in advance.

events.title: A radio target drone is shown to the army
events.who: Reginald Denny and his Radioplane company
events.text: In 1935 the company demonstrated a prototype radio-controlled target drone, the RP-1, to the US Army. Targets like these let gunners practise on a moving aircraft without a pilot in danger.
events.why: Radio control was made practical for everyday, repeated flights, not just for experiments.

events.title: The first army order for radio targets
events.text: The US Army placed its first order with Radioplane in 1940, for 53 RP-4 target drones. A larger order for the RP-5, which became the OQ-2, followed in 1941.
events.why: A government order turned radio-controlled flight into a product that could be built in numbers.

events.title: Nearly 15,000 target drones in the war
events.text: During the Second World War Radioplane built nearly fifteen thousand of its drones. Most were used as moving targets to train anti-aircraft crews.
events.why: It was one of the first unmanned aircraft built in large numbers.

events.title: The first quadcopter with a camera
events.who: Makers of toy and research quadcopters
events.text: Small toy quadcopters were already sold in Japan in the early 1990s. The first quadcopter with a camera made in significant numbers was not designed until 1999.
events.why: A camera turned the four-rotor toy into a machine that could look at the world from the air.

events.title: Cheap sensors make the quadcopter practical
events.text: Around 2005 to 2010, electronics became cheap and light enough to make small flight controllers. The quadcopter layout then became popular for small unmanned aircraft.
events.why: A gyroscope and accelerometer on a small chip could do the feedback loop that keeps a drone level (chapter 2).

events.title: India notifies the Drone Rules, 2021
events.text: The Ministry of Civil Aviation notified the Drone Rules, 2021 in the Gazette on 25 August 2021. The rules sort drones by all-up weight, cover drones up to 500 kg, and run registration on the Digital Sky platform.
events.why: It set the weight classes, the zones and the registration that drones still follow, and the 2022 and 2023 amendments built on it.

events.title: India publishes its drone airspace map
events.text: The Prime Minister released India's airspace map for drones on 24 September 2021. It shows the red and yellow zones, and anyone can view it on Digital Sky without a login.
events.why: Drone pilots must check the live map before every flight, because zone boundaries can change.

events.title: A certification scheme for drones
events.text: A notification of 26 January 2022 published the certification scheme for unmanned aircraft systems, which sets how new drone models are approved.
events.why: Type certification checks that a drone model is safe before it is sold or flown.

events.title: Drones carry vaccines to remote areas
events.where: Manipur, Nagaland and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands
events.text: An ICMR-led pilot project to carry COVID-19 vaccines by drone was being rolled out in Manipur, Nagaland, and the Andaman and Nicobar Islands.
events.why: Drones can reach places where roads are poor or cut off.

events.title: First amendment to the Drone Rules
events.text: An amendment dated 11 February 2022 changed the rule on remote pilot certificates and gave owners of drones made or imported by 30 November 2021 until 31 March 2022 to register them.
events.why: Amendments change the rules, so pilots and owners must check the current text.

events.title: The Kisan Drone scheme for farmers
events.who: Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers Welfare
events.text: At its launch in May 2022, the government offered farmers subsidies to buy drones for spraying and mapping. Press reports gave 50% of the cost, up to Rs 5 lakh, for SC-ST, small, marginal and women farmers. This is from press reports and has not been checked at source.
events.why: Spraying by drone covers a field quickly and keeps the operator away from the chemical.

events.title: A second amendment widens who can be a pilot
events.text: An amendment dated 27 September 2023 let applicants use other government-issued identity and address proofs, such as a voter ID or driving licence, on the registration form. This is from the amendment's summary, not checked clause by clause.
events.why: Registration became simpler, but the rules on flying still apply.

events.title: Namo Drone Didi
events.who: Ministries of agriculture, rural development and fertilisers
events.text: The Namo Drone Didi scheme aims to give drones to 15,000 women's self-help groups over 2024-25 and 2025-26. The groups rent the drones to farmers, mostly to spray liquid fertiliser and pesticide. The Centre covers 80% of the cost, up to Rs 8 lakh per drone.
events.why: It turns drone flying into a source of income for rural women, with training built in.

facts: A quadcopter has no swashplate: the speed of each rotor does the steering.
Two propellers turn clockwise and two anticlockwise, so their twists cancel and the body stays still.
India's green airspace for drones runs up to 400 feet (120 m), the same height limit as the FAA's Part 107.
Under the Drone Rules, 2021, a drone's class depends on its all-up weight, payload included.
